paper_title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real-world professional tasks. Short trajectories can demonstrate commands and tool calls, but they do not fully show how agents accumulate evidence through exploration, use it to inform judgments, continually adjust strategies based on feedback, and turn intermediate results into final deliverables. High-quality long-horizon trajectories capture these agentic behavioral patterns and their connections within a single problem-solving process, providing richer experience for sustained autonomous work. However, environment synthesis may complete or simplify the key work underlying these patterns in advance and thus remove the need for exploration, implementation, and verification that the agent was meant to perform. To address this, we introduce TerminalHorizon, a fully automated data synthesis engine for long-horizon terminal agents. Starting from real-world professional work, it uses independent execution to identify key work omitted during construction and uses the resulting evidence to guide environment reconstruction. To extend these patterns across stages, it progressively expands tasks under the same goal, introducing new requirements that build on prior results and call for further exploration and improvement. Using this engine, we construct 1.5K task environments and perform supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on the resulting dataset to obtain TerminalHorizon-27B. We achieve substantial performance gains on all 12 benchmarks spanning coding-agent tasks, agentic tasks in real-world production settings, and general reasoning. Multiple RSI case studies, each with a 12-hour research budget, further demonstrate the model's ability to continue experimenting beyond an initial solution, improve its methods based on feedback, and retain effective improvements in its final deliverables.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: LLM agents are moving beyond answering questions in dialogue toward autonomous work in digital environments (Xu et al., 2026; Koh et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2026). The terminal provides general interface for this work by bringing code, data, tools, and execution feedback into shared workspace (Merrill et al., 2026), enabling agents to tackle complex tasks in software development, system administration, and scientific computing (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2025). As their scope expands from individual operations to long-horizon tasks (Dong et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026; Qwen Team, 2026; Ye et al., 2025), agents need to coordinate interdependent stages and adapt to execution feedback to complete these tasks reliably (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Desai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Developing these capabilities requires rich interaction experience during training, but high-quality terminal training data remains scarce. sections.content: Figure 1: Motivation for TerminalHorizon. Short trajectories can teach agents to perform terminal operations, but not to autonomously complete complex, long-horizon tasks. Our long-horizon trajectories connect agentic behavioral patterns, such as exploration, strategy revision, and verification, into complete autonomous problem-solving process. allowing agents to gain interaction experience through execution and feedback (Wu et al., 2026a; Cheng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026b; Fan et al., 2026). These methods expand task coverage, but their trajectories remain relatively short on average as shown in Figure 4, offering limited experience in sustained problem solving. Short trajectories can capture useful agentic behavioral patterns over few steps, but the same patterns can extend across multiple stages or even an entire trajectory in long-horizon tasks. For example, agents may repeatedly revise their plans as evidence accumulates, build on intermediate results through sequence of dependent steps, and revisit earlier work when later verification reveals problems that require further diagnosis and correction. This motivates our focus on high-quality long-horizon trajectories that capture these longer agentic behavioral patterns and show how they work together to complete task (Section 3). However, synthesizing these long-horizon trajectories presents two challenges. (i) Complex tasks do not necessarily lead to the intended agentic behavioral patterns. task may require agents to investigate problem, develop solution, and verify it, yet supplied materials may already solve parts of the problem, allowing agents to skip exploration or implementation. These gaps can prevent the intended patterns from fully developing in the collected trajectories. (ii) Even when these patterns appear, long-horizon training data should also capture how they unfold over longer problem-solving processes and connect across stages. More difficult tasks or more interaction turns do not necessarily extend these patterns or strengthen their connections. The challenge is to identify and implement new requirements that go beyond what the original solution can achieve, while keeping the same goal. The added work needs to build on earlier judgments, actions, and results, so that these patterns continue to develop as the task progresses. To this end, we introduce TerminalHorizon, fully automated data synthesis engine with two stages: Challenge-Guided Long-Horizon Synthesis and Progressive Horizon Expansion. The first stage converts real-world professional problems into executable tasks and uses an agent uninvolved in their construction to solve them. Analysis of the resulting trajectories checks whether the intended agentic behavioral patterns occur and identifies where task construction has simplified or already completed the analysis, implementation, or verification expected of the agent. These findings guide environment reconstruction so that the agent must perform this work during execution. The second stage expands the original task under the same goal, introducing requirements that call for further analysis, implementation, and verification. It makes this added work depend on earlier results and execution feedback, allowing the intended patterns to extend across stages. Together, these stages support the generation of long-horizon trajectories in which the intended agentic behavioral patterns emerge and extend across stages toward task completion. Using TerminalHorizon, we construct 1,535 task environments and collect 2,852 training trajectories to form TerminalHorizon-3K. The trajectories average 52.8 interaction turns, substantially longer than those from the methods compared in Figure 4. Supervised Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on these 2,852 trajectories yields TerminalHorizon-27B, which improves over the base model by 14.2% and 13.85% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1, respectively. These gains extend to real-world productivity tasks, with improvements of 11.7% in Pass Rate and 23.3% in Partial score on AutomationBench, and 11.3% on VitaBench. sections.title: 3 ANALYSIS OF SYNTHESIZED DATA
sections.content: The following analysis illustrates the training experience provided by TerminalHorizon: our model can learn not only how to execute terminal commands but, more importantly, how to organize sustained work toward goal, observe feedback, revise strategies, and deliver final results.

sections.content: Figure 3: Comprehensive analysis of task environments and trajectories in TerminalHorizon. Trajectory Collection. We use TerminalHorizon to automatically generate 1,535 task environment packages and collect two trajectories per task using DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 as the teacher model and Terminus2 as the execution harness. We then apply the three filtering criteria described in Appendix F, retaining 2,852 trajectories to form TerminalHorizon-3K. We conduct rigorous benchmark decontamination before training (Appendix G). Broad coverage of real-world domains. As shown in Figure 3a, TerminalHorizon-3K brings realworld work in areas such as chips, physics, and astronomy into unified terminal interaction format, covering 25 professional domains. This diversity is enabled by the Planner Agents scheduling and coordination throughout the automated construction process. See Appendix for details. Sustained interaction. For fair comparison, we randomly sample 300 tasks from each of several open-source terminaltask synthesis methods and run experiments under the same teacher protocol and settings. Our trajectories have mean interaction length of 52.8 turns and 90th percentile of 98 turns, substantially exceeding those of other methods (Figure 4). We also measure the longest continuous action chain linked by terminal feedback to examine how long feedback remains part of the interaction. Figure 3c shows median chain length of 25 turns. These results show that longer execution includes sustained sequences of actions and environment feedback, demonstrating how to connect observations with subsequent actions across multiple turns. Figure 4: Interaction turns per trajectory: mean, P50, and P90. Agentic behavioral patterns beyond individual commands. Beyond interaction length, we examine how these actions organize problem solving. As shown in Figure 3d, we group 27 behavioral patterns into five categories: information exploration and judgment, diagnosis and error correction, construction and work progress, verification and assurance, and strategy and execution coordination. These patterns describe how agents organize multi-step actions into problem-solving process. For example, subproblem decomposition and integration breaks task into subproblems and combines their results to achieve shared goal. Detailed pattern definitions are provided in Appendix E. Our trajectories contain an average of 8.6 core patterns, providing diverse behavioral experience spanning exploration, construction, error correction, and verification.

Taking multi-view point cloud fusion as an example, Figure 7 shows both models optimization processes and final results. The base model obtains high score on self-designed proxy metric and voluntarily stops after just 12.1 minutes, judging its results to be excellent and ready for submission. However, agreement with single reference view does not ensure reconstruction of the complete scene: method can perform well on this proxy while missing surfaces visible only in other views. In contrast, our model continues experimenting beyond the initial solution and revisits both its fusion method and the measurements used to assess progress. It inspects the contributions of different views and introduces leave-one-view-out diagnostic, which exposes insufficient coverage and guides subsequent revisions. It then improves cross-view alignment, performs global refinement, and uses confidence-based point selection to improve the reconstruction. These changes reflect substantive revisions informed by experimental evidence, rather than simply repeating the same operations for longer. Our model retains the resulting improvements in its final submission, whose hidden evaluation score exceeds the base models by 27.03%. This comparison illustrates the practical value of experience with agentic behavioral patterns: connecting exploration, diagnosis, method revision, and verification enables agents to keep seeking improvements and turn verified progress into final deliverables. Additional cases are provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Long-Horizon Agents. Long-horizon agents must retain information, track progress, and coordinate actions across stages (Dong et al., 2026b; Ren et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Harnesses support execution through context, memory, and state management, helping maintain continuity during extended interactions (Ye et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026). We complement this support by studying how training develops sustained problem-solving ability, particularly the agentic behavioral patterns that connect exploration, implementation, and verification around shared goal. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced TerminalHorizon, fully automated engine for synthesizing long-horizon trajectories that connect agentic behavioral patterns. Through challenge-guided reconstruction and progressive expansion, it links exploration, strategy revision, and verification around shared goal. Training on these trajectories improves performance on all 12 benchmarks, while RSI-Exam cases show sustained experimentation, feedback-driven improvement, and progress retained through final delivery. These findings highlight the training value of long-horizon behavioral experience in advancing agents from local terminal operations toward sustained autonomous work.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI for automated task environment construction and solution trajectory generation as part of our research methodology, and for language polishing and the generation of selected illustration assets during manuscript preparation. The procedures and validation mechanisms for task environment construction and trajectory generation are described in the Method section and the appendix. We did not use generative AI to formulate research questions, develop the core research ideas, or design the research methodology. We manually reviewed all AI-assisted content. For language polishing, we checked that the revised wording preserved the intended meaning. For generated illustration assets, we checked that they accurately conveyed the relevant concepts without introducing misleading information. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and illustration assets produced with the aid of generative AI. ETHICS STATEMENT This work studies long-horizon task learning for terminal agents through synthetic task environments, generated solution trajectories, and benchmark evaluations, examining how sustained interaction experience affects agent capabilities. Within the scope of this study, we have identified no significant ethical concerns requiring specific disclosure. The procedures for task construction, data filtering, and experimental evaluation are detailed in the main text and the appendix. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT To support reproducibility, we describe the task formulation and two-stage synthesis procedure in Section 2, and trajectory collection and experimental settings in Section 3 and Section 4. Appendix A.1 provides the training configuration, while Appendix A.2 specifies the benchmark protocols, including agent frameworks, decoding settings, interaction limits, and scoring procedures. Trajectory filtering and benchmark decontamination are described in Appendices and G, with the corresponding prompt templates in Appendix J. For the long-horizon RSI case studies, Appendix details the research setup, evaluation procedure, and evidence underlying the case analyses.

All evaluated models are served through vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) on eight H20 GPUs, with tensor parallelism degree of 8 and context window of 262,144 tokens. For each benchmark, the base and TerminalHorizon models use the same task set, agent framework, decoding settings, and scoring procedure. Terminal-Bench, AutomationBench, and general reasoning evaluations use temperature of 1.0, top-p = 0.95, top-k = 20, and maximum of 65,536 output tokens per response. Decoding settings for VitaBench and τ 2-bench are specified below. Terminal-Bench. We evaluate on Terminal-Bench 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) using Harbor2 and Terminus-2 with JSON parser. Terminal-Bench 1.0 contains 80 tasks and uses Daytona sandboxes, each allocated 2 CPUs, 4 GiB of memory, and 8 GiB of storage. Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1 each contain 89 tasks and use E2B sandboxes. All three versions allow the agent three hours per task, while verifiers retain the time limits specified by each task. Terminus-2 triggers proactive summarization when the estimated remaining context capacity falls below 131,072 tokens. We run each task independently three times and report mean pass@1, with up to two retries for infrastructure errors. AutomationBench. We evaluate AutomationBench v1.0.6 (Shepard & Salimans, 2026) with 600 rollouts over the full public set, using the official api tool set and limit of 50 steps per trajectory. Each model is evaluated in three independent runs, and we report the mean official Partial score (the fraction of assertions passed) and Pass Rate (all assertions passed). Interrupted samples are retried for up to three rounds; samples that remain incomplete receive score of zero. VitaBench Cross-domain. We use the main English Cross-domain set of VitaBench 1.0 (He et al., 2025), which contains 100 tasks spanning food delivery, in-store services, and travel. The agent must estimate spatially varying seabed friction field from bathymetry, boundary forcing, and sparse observations of complex tidal elevation. Some gauges contain large, unmarked observation errors. Because the forward simulator smooths the effect of friction changes on tidal elevation, the inverse problem is ill-posed: fitting the observed gauges does not guarantee accurate predictions elsewhere. The submitted solver must return bounded 24 24 log-friction field. Development uses six public basins, and final evaluation uses eight hidden cases. Figure 11 shows the research process, spatial error comparisons, and results on all eight hidden basins. Revising the model of the inverse problem. The base model recognizes the need for spatial regularization and outlier handling, adopting 4 4 bilinear parameterization, coordinate descent, and iterative residual-based observation rejection. After achieving public mean RMSE of 0.023616, it voluntarily stops after 1.12 hours. TerminalHorizon27B instead continues to compare spatial bases, robust losses, and regularization methods rather than treating the initial parameterization as fixed. sections.content: C.4 MULTI-VIEW POINT-CLOUD FUSION Task and source of difficulty. The agent must reconstruct complete scene by fusing noisy point clouds from partially overlapping views. The first view defines the reference coordinate frame, while the remaining views contain unknown small rigid transformations; each observed point also has confidence value. The agent must align the views, suppress unreliable points, and preserve surface coverage within fixed output-size limit. The public self-check only verifies compliance with the output interface and provides neither ground-truth geometry nor reconstruction quality scores. Final evaluation uses nine unseen scenes and averages symmetric precisionrecall F-scores over three distance tolerances, penalizing both inaccurate points and missing surface regions. Figure 13 shows the five remaining scenes (02, 04, 06, 07, and 08), complementing scenes 01, 03, 05, and 09 in Figure 7. These visualizations compare final submissions rather than intermediate research versions. Questioning what proxy actually measures. After trying iterative closest point alignment, the base model settles on conservative approach: it translates the other views toward the reference views centroid and retains only points close to that view. It obtains high F-score on self-designed proxy metric and voluntarily stops after 12.1 minutes. Specifically, it describes the results as excellent based on mean proxy F-score of 0.8994 and proxy F-score of 1.0 at the 0.05 distance threshold for every case, concluding that the solver is ready to submit. However, agreement with the reference observation is not equivalent to agreement with the complete scene. Selecting points close to single view can raise this proxy score while omitting surfaces visible only in other views. TerminalHorizon27B encounters similar issue in early experiments. variant that selects points by nearest distance to the reference view achieves proxy score of about 0.989, but the agent inspects which views contribute the selected points and questions whether the metric rewards reconstruction or merely copying the reference view. It then introduces leave-one-view-out diagnostic, identifies poor coverage of the excluded view, and revises its fusion strategy accordingly. Aligning the method with geometric coverage. TerminalHorizon-27Bs final solver filters nearestpoint correspondences by distance threshold, estimates rotation and translation through rigid alignment, and jointly refines each non-reference view against the other aligned views. It performs two rounds of global refinement and selects high-confidence points from the merged cloud, rather than restricting added points to the area near the first view. In the official hidden evaluation, the mean F-score across distance tolerances, expressed on 0100 scale, increases from 48.04 to 77.68; the separately calibrated normalized score rises from 21.93 to 48.96. The key behavioral difference is the agents willingness to revise not only the solver but also the experiments used to assess progress. Interface validity and high proxy scores provide only intermediate evidence, while cross-view diagnostics help align the method with the actual reconstruction objective. Together, these four cases illustrate complementary aspects of sustained autonomous research: jointly optimizing coupled objectives, revising scientific models, testing and reverting search heuristics, and identifying misleading proxy metrics. They share close connection between observations, subsequent decisions, and the implementation ultimately submitted for evaluation. Longer interaction is valuable when it supports these connections, rather than serving as an objective in itself.

sections.title: G DETAILED BENCHMARK DECONTAMINATION
sections.content: Direct reuse or close paraphrasing of evaluation problems in training tasks can make it difficult to distinguish capability gains from memorization. To assess this risk, we compare all 1,535 training tasks with the evaluation benchmarks at the task level, combining exact-span matching, near-duplicate retrieval, and semantic assessment to identify potential task overlap. G.1 COMPARISON CORPORA The comparison corpora cover 3,251 evaluation instances across 12 benchmark groups: TerminalBench 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1; AutomationBench; the English Cross-domain tasks in VitaBench; τ 2bench Airline and Retail; MATH-500; GSM8K; AIME 2024; AIME 2025; and KOR-Bench Cipher. Each training task is represented by its full instruction.md, while each evaluation instance is represented by its problem statement or user request. Table 8 lists the sources and fields used. The comparison texts retain the task objectives and necessary context. For KOR-Bench Cipher, we combine the cipher rules with the question. For VitaBench and τ 2-bench, we use the full user-request scenario, preserving its goals, known information, and constraints, including requirements that may be disclosed gradually during interaction. No text is summarized or truncated, and reference answers, private scoring criteria, and expected execution outcomes are excluded from the comparison. G.2 TEXT OVERLAP AND NEAR-DUPLICATE RETRIEVAL We apply Unicode NFKC normalization and lowercasing to the task descriptions, then tokenize them into contiguous sequences of Unicode letters, digits, and underscores. Exact matching covers both the full normalized text and contiguous 13-token and 14-token windows with stride of 1. Let Gn(x) denote the set of contiguous n-grams in task description x. Exact-span overlap between training description and an evaluation description is defined as En(x, y) = I[Gn(x) Gn(y) = ] , {13, 14}. (9) To retrieve near-duplicate tasks that do not share long verbatim spans, we also compute the Jaccard similarity between their 5-gram sets, J5(x, y) = G5(x) G5(y) G5(x) G5(y) , (10) and the cosine similarity STF(x, y) between their unigram/bigram TFIDF representations. The former captures local phrase reuse, while the latter captures lexical similarity under changes in word order. TFIDF is fitted on the combined corpus of training tasks and the benchmark being compared, using logarithmic term frequency and smoothed inverse document frequency. For mathematical and symbolic expressions, we additionally retrieve contiguous 8-gram overlaps using tokenizer that preserves LATEX commands, numbers, and operators. Because these short spans may represent common formulas or interfaces, they supplement candidate retrieval rather than directly establish contamination. We also report base-2 unigram JensenShannon divergence (JSD) to characterize differences in word distributions between the training corpus and each benchmark; this metric is not used to determine contamination. None of the 12 benchmark groups contains an exact match to normalized full text or contiguous 13/14-token window. The maximum 5-gram Jaccard similarity is 0.006024, and the maximum TFIDF cosine similarity is 0.083445. Math-aware 8-gram retrieval identifies 405 pairs with short-span overlap, which are used for candidate selection alongside lexical nearest neighbors. After combining and deduplicating the retrieval results, 190 candidate pairs undergo semantic review; none is classified as contaminated or uncertain. These comparisons of task descriptions and semantic assessments find no evidence of evaluation-task reuse in the training tasks, so all 1,535 training tasks are retained. CASE STUDIES OF CHALLENGE-GUIDED RECONSTRUCTION We examine three cases of numerical calibration, distributed-service recovery, and household benefits administration in which independent challenges exposed work lost during environment construction. Each traces the initial execution, the resulting reconstruction, and the work observed in subsequent independent challenge.

sections.content: H.1 RADIO-INTERFEROMETRIC CALIBRATION The agent must calibrate synthetic Northstar-10 radio observation stored as native MeasurementSet while preserving the raw measurements and metadata. Calibration is evaluated on holdout and target data excluded from fitting. The environment uses casacore, NumPy, and SciPy for data access and numerical computation. Case 1 Restoring numerical calibration work 01 Initial construction The public mscal tool included solve-bandpass and solve-gain, which performed numerical fitting and wrote native calibration tables, so core implementation work was already packaged into the environment. 02 Independent challenge: successful, but compressed After identifying the fields, the challenger invoked the bundled solvers, applied the calibration, and checked residuals. It adjusted the fitted field selection after failed check, but did not need to implement the numerical calibration. 03 Reconstruction: leave the fit to the agent Reconstruction removed the fitting routines but retained inspection, calibration application, and residual feedback. It introduced distinct time-varying responses for the two spectral windows and made the required solution axes and table conventions public. 04 Independent re-challenge: feedback changes the model The fresh challenger inspected the data axes and public interfaces, implemented fitting workflow, and revised its spectral-window-dependent parameters after observing high residuals. It wrote and applied native calibration tables, checked that the raw data remained unchanged, and evaluated holdout and target data without fitting them. Final weighted RMS was 0.896 on the fitted calibrators, 1.784 on holdout, and 1.944 on target, all below the public threshold of 2.8. The independent run passed the verifier. These scores describe the reconstructed task, not comparison between task versions. What reconstruction restores. The initial challenger also passed, showing that task success alone does not reveal work completed in advance. Reconstruction moved numerical modeling and implementation from the supplied tool to the agent while retaining the interfaces and feedback needed to complete the task. The resulting trajectory connects model construction, residual-driven revision, and independent validation. H.2 RABBITMQ RECOVERY ACROSS BROKER AND APPLICATION STATE The agent must recover three-node RabbitMQ service from network partition while preserving confirmed messages, resolving failed or uncertain publications, and preventing duplicate business effects. The synthetic incident runs on real RabbitMQ brokers and AMQP clients, with firewall rules and persistent application state. Five reconstruction rounds and six independent challenges turned application recovery from possible branch into work required by the running environment. Case 2 From broker recovery to application recovery 01 Initial challenge: recovery is largely prebuilt The challenger used the supplied partitionctl heal, restarted one broker, and let the clients finish. Automatic retry and idempotent consumption handled much of the application recovery, leaving short operational path.

sections.content: 02 Rounds 12: reconstruct the live recovery state The redesigns removed the healing command and introduced three queues with different missing voting replicas. Missing members and network faults were selected from live broker state rather than fixed repair map. Unresolved publications were kept in durable outbox, and recovery had to preserve unrelated firewall policy. 03 Round 3: restore dependencies within application work The workload changed from independent messages to 27 workflows of eight ordered operations. Publishers retained event identities for reconciliation and resumption; consumers tracked predecessor completion and prevented duplicate business effects. The intended recovery now depended on both broker health and the completion of earlier workflow steps. 04 Repeated challenges: the new work still does not occur Intermediate challenges still finished without the intended reconciliation work. One run encountered no uncertain publications; in later run, the client could reach its local queue leader despite the partition. The recovery branch existed but was not needed in either execution. 05 Rounds 45: connect the fault to its application consequence The redesigns moved fault installation before client startup and connected the orders client to runtime-selected follower whose leader was across the partition. The actual AMQP path now exposed the application failure that earlier versions could avoid. 06 Final independent challenge: recover the missing predecessor After restoring connectivity and queue voters, the challenger found 71 confirmed orders rows and one nacked first-step event, with downstream consumer errors. It retrieved the stored message body and original event ID, then republished with AMQP publisher confirms. All 216 outbox rows became confirmed, every workflow reached step 8, and no duplicate business effects were observed. The independent run passed. What reconstruction restores. Reconstruction linked network and replica repair to unfinished application work. Repeated challenges showed that recovery branch adds no workload unless the running environment actually triggers it. The final run had to recover specific missing event before dependent workflow steps could finish. H.3 FAMILY ENROLLMENT CHANGES AND PAYROLL RECONCILIATION This case concerns household coverage change following the loss of other insurance. The agent must assess dependent eligibility and keep benefits enrollment, payroll deductions, and insurer records consistent. The household, rules, and service are synthetic, modeling an employers benefits workflow through stateful public interfaces. Four reconstruction rounds and five independent challenges developed simple record-update task into evidence-based review and coordinated updates across systems. Case 3 From enrollment edits to evidence-based reconciliation 01 Initial challenge: fixed update sequence After inspecting the case, the challenger amended three plans, denied one dependent, and synchronized payroll and insurer records. Most extra interactions came from discovering command syntax, not from analyzing evidence or revising decisions. 02 Rounds 12: connect coverage dates to downstream records Previously posted deductions now required retroactive payroll adjustments. dependents age limit split coverage into consecutive periods, changing pay-period calculations and insurer payloads. Legacy insurer plan codes also had to be updated before the new records could be accepted.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 03 Round 3: revise an already accepted case The starting state now contained committed enrollment, applied payroll, and an accepted insurer transaction, followed by corrected dependent document. The agent had to reopen the case, create replacement version, and update both downstream systems without erasing the earlier records. 04 Re-challenge: the evidence decision is still supplied The corrected document was already marked verified, the affected person was obvious, and each downstream issue had one clear remedy. The challenger could still follow fixed sequence once it had read the case. Versioned updates alone had not restored the intended evidence analysis. 05 Round 4: make review outcomes change the decision Reconstruction introduced conflicting document claims and their source records. One dependent had both mismatching document and corroborating alternative; another had an authentic document whose loss date failed the event-date rule. Public review and validation returned feedback that determined which people could be included in the revised coverage. 06 Final independent challenge: revise and propagate the decision The challenger rejected mismatching evidence, found the corroborating source, and revised its provisional enrollment after validation exposed the ineligible loss date. It approved D-4, denied D-3 and D-5, and preserved the age-bounded coverage for D-2. It then committed version 6, applied $312 payroll adjustment, and obtained insurer acceptance while retaining version 5. The independent run passed. What reconstruction restores. The key change is that document review now determines the next action rather than confirming decision already supplied by the environment. An authentic document can still fail the eligibility rule, and an unsupported claim requires another source. Once the household decision changes, its effective dates and source version must remain consistent across enrollment, payroll, and insurer acceptance. The final trajectory therefore connects evidence comparison, feedback-driven revision, and verified updates across systems.

sections.title: J PROMPT TEMPLATES
sections.content: J.1 TRAJECTORY FILTERING PROMPT The following prompt implements the three filtering criteria in Appendix by reviewing complete trajectories and returning an evidence-backed KEEP/DROP decision for each input record. Trajectory Filtering Prompt You are an expert reviewer of terminal-agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Your task is to determine whether each complete multi-turn trajectory provides reliable and useful training example. Read the entire conversation. Do not substitute excerpts, keyword counts, command counts, or programmatic summaries for the original trajectory. Base your judgment exclusively on the trajectory itself. Do not access task packages, private verifiers, external benchmarks, or the internet. Understanding the trajectory - The initial user message typically contains the task description and the agent interaction protocol. - Subsequent user messages usually contain terminal observations produced by preceding commands, rather than new user requests.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: - Assistant messages contain reasoning, plans, and terminal actions. One assistant turn may contain multiple commands. - Reasoning, including <think>, analysis, and plan content, is not itself evidence of execution. Evaluate it together with the actual actions and subsequent observations. - Terminus-2 trajectory may end with the terminal observation from its final command batch. This is normal ending and does not require an additional assistant confirmation. - Final success or failure is not sufficient to determine training value. An incomplete trajectory or an honest stopping point at an unresolved obstacle may still provide useful demonstration. Evaluate only the following three dimensions. 1. Trajectory validity Is the trajectory coherent and correctly ordered? Can actions be reliably associated with their terminal observations? Check for genuine context truncation, severe format corruption, execution in the wrong container, infrastructure failures, explicit refusal, or private-answer leakage that compromises the demonstration. Do not reject an entire trajectory because of one or two isolated invalid JSON responses, malformed commands, or parser errors. If the agent recognizes the problem, restores valid interaction, and continues with clear actionobservation chain, this constitutes learnable recovery process. Treat protocol errors as an overall validity defect when they recur without reliable recovery or make actionobservation correspondence uninterpretable. Protocol recovery does not excuse independent integrity violations. Reject trajectories whose core solution relies on private answers or hidden-test leakage, internal-state tampering, deleting runtime or database state to reset the task, or bypassing required task interfaces. Distinguish failure to finish from lack of training value. An unfinished trajectory can be retained when its main content demonstrates reliable environment understanding, root-cause diagnosis, justified implementation, feedback-based elimination of alternatives, correction of assumptions, or identification of unresolved obstacles. An isolated incorrect final judgment or unsupported completion claim does not automatically invalidate all preceding work. Determine whether the error compromises the core action chain. Retention is possible when the main process remains reliable and useful. Reject the trajectory when an incorrect strategy dominates the solution, central conclusions contradict observations, or the overall example primarily demonstrates an invalid way to complete the task. 2. Environment-grounded progress Are important actions supported by actual terminal feedback? Does the agent use files, logs, command outputs, errors, and test results to advance the task and adjust its approach when necessary? Identify persistent disregard of feedback, repeated ineffective commands, random attempts, unmotivated minor edits, and unsupported completion claims. Evaluate these behaviors in context: unsuccessful attempts can be valuable when their observations inform subsequent diagnosis, revision, or recovery. 3. Multi-turn training value Does the trajectory demonstrate multi-turn terminal problem-solving process worth learning? Do interactions contribute meaningful evidence, implementation, state changes, decisions, verification, or recovery? Consider whether the apparent interaction could be trivially replaced by one obvious edit, fixed script, or mechanical loop. Do not count SSH, Docker, or Harbor infrastructure operations, waiting, repeated polling, or irrelevant directory browsing as evidence of task difficulty. Do not judge training value solely from trajectory length, command count, the presence of mistakes, or final task success. Decision KEEP: The trajectory is valid, grounded in the environment, and provides sufficient multi-turn training value. Final failure, incomplete execution, or an honest stopping point does not preclude KEEP when the main process is reliable and instructive. DROP: The trajectory is globally invalid; its core solution relies on leakage, state tampering, or interface bypass; its behavior substantially degenerates or lacks environmental grounding; or errors dominate the main action chain with little reliable multi-turn learning value.

Benchmark Decontamination Prompt Role and objective You are an expert reviewer of contamination between training data and evaluation benchmarks. Compare each candidate Terminal/CLI task with its paired public evaluation problem to determine whether the candidate leaks, copies, or substantially reproduces that problem. Read the complete descriptions of every pair in assigned-pairs.jsonl. Similarity scores are retrieval signals, not conclusions. Assessment criteria Determine whether exposure to the training candidate would make the evaluation problem substantially easier because the two are the same or nearly the same task. Compare their core objectives, initial problems, key objects or data, required transformations, distinctive constraints, key solution paths, and final completion criteria. - CONTAMINATED: direct copy or minor rewording, or renamed task that retains sufficiently distinctive instance details, constraint combinations, and solution structure to remain substantially the same problem. - CLEAN: The tasks share only domain, tools, general terminology, or common professional work patterns; their specific instances, states, constraints, and required work are independent. - UNCERTAIN: The evidence is genuinely close, but the public descriptions alone do not permit reliable distinction. Do not classify ordinary topical similarity as UNCERTAIN. Phrase overlap arising only from templates, common interfaces, mathematical notation, or standard industry expressions does not constitute contamination. Conversely, the absence of long n-gram overlap does not rule out systematic rewrite of the same instance.
